measurement.happened:
This week in Russia was dominated by a dramatic shift in the diplomatic track, punctuated by continued heavy fighting on the ground. The single biggest story was the resumption of peace negotiations. On October 21, the Kremlin confirmed that Putin agreed to resume three-way talks with Ukraine and the United States, after US envoy Steve Witkoff met with Putin in St. Petersburg. Zelensky confirmed that Ukrainian, Russian, and US negotiators would meet in Abu Dhabi in early November. This was framed as a major breakthrough, and the Kremlin called the moment 'historic.' However, the talks were overshadowed by fighting: within hours of Putin's agreement, Russia dropped cluster warheads on Kyiv and both sides traded overnight strikes. Zelensky said Russia's continued attacks showed 'no change in attitude,' and Ukraine launched over 1,000 drones at Russia, setting oil facilities ablaze and hitting data centers of Russia's largest bank. The war remained very much active despite the diplomatic overture.

A second major thread was the US-Russia energy and sanctions deal. Trump waived several Russian sanctions just before a new law took effect, a move that outraged both Democrats and many Republicans in Congress. The first tanker of Russian diesel under the Trump-Putin deal set sail for the US on October 23, with delivery expected in 15 to 20 days. Oil futures pulled back on the news, and Morgan Stanley estimated the deal would provide roughly 12 hours of US diesel supply. The deal was politically contentious: Trump defended it as an incentive for peace, while Zelensky called it an 'encouragement' for Putin. Novatek, the Russian gas giant, was revealed to have funded a US LNG project, and US executives quit a 25-billion-dollar gas venture over claims of secret Russian control. The deal also touched on Lukoil's foreign assets, which Russia and the US discussed.

A third theme was the one-city ceasefire in Oleshky, brokered by Melania Trump. Russia and Ukraine agreed to a temporary ceasefire around the Russian-occupied town to allow humanitarian aid and civilian evacuation. The Kremlin confirmed it was working with Ukraine on evacuation timing. This was a small but symbolic de-escalation, and the US said both sides would let civilians leave the war-torn area. However, Zelensky remained doubtful about Russian acceptance of a broader 'energy ceasefire.'

The release of 74-year-old American Stephen Hubbard, who had been in a Russian jail for over four years, was a major human-interest story. Hubbard arrived back in the US on October 22. Russia and Ukraine also swapped 270 prisoners each. The release was tied to the Witkoff-Putin meeting and seen as a goodwill gesture, though Russia and the US later clarified that Hubbard was not formally exchanged for a Russian war blogger.

Espionage and intelligence activity was another prominent thread. Austria expelled four Russian diplomats linked to espionage. A suspected Russian spy was arrested in Germany, and Chancellor Merz warned Europe it was underestimating the Russian threat. Russia arrested a German man it called a Ukrainian 'mercenary' and also detained a Japanese journalist, the latest sign of deteriorating Russia-Japan ties. In space, a Russian military satellite made an unprecedented close approach to a US radar satellite used by Ukraine, raising concerns about orbital stalking. Poland said social media firms were a 'silent ally' of Russia and threatened fines, while Germany's military warned of a 'significant' Russian sabotage threat.

On the economic front, Russia's central bank kept its key rate on hold at 14 percent and raised its 2026 inflation forecast, citing Ukrainian strikes on energy infrastructure as a driver. Russian oil used for tax calculations jumped 60 percent above the budget level. Russia shipped the least oil in a month after a major Baltic port halted operations. Russia also turned to a disputed region to keep wheat exports flowing, and global wheat futures rose on supply fears. Nestle removed Russian business from its accounts after a Kremlin takeover of a unit, and Russia's temporary control of a metro unit was reported to be reaping funds for the war effort.

The war itself saw continued intensity. Russia stepped up attacks on Ukraine's digital infrastructure and energy grid. A Russian drone killed a toddler and her mother in a Ukrainian park. Romania blamed Russia for a drone that sank a cargo ship in the Black Sea, killing one and leaving three missing. Ukraine struck Moscow-area airports, targeting Russia's aviation and travel sectors. Russia built a new jet-powered drone launch megabase in just six weeks. North Korean workers were reported to be treated as 'slaves' at a Russian drone factory. In Mali, Human Rights Watch accused the army and its Russian allies of new atrocities against civilians.

Diplomatic and political reactions across Europe were sharp. Slovakia broke with EU allies by restarting consultations with Russia. Hungary considered replacing Rosatom in a nuclear project. Latvia called for a visa ban on Russians. Finland sought one million land mines as it eyes the Russian threat. The EU unveiled a new Arctic strategy in response to Russian and US pressure. The UK warned of gaps in its Arctic defense. Poland renewed its Cold War bunkers in preparation for Russian hybrid attacks. Denmark ordered long-range missiles, drawing Russian ire. In Serbia, a vote pitted a Putin-backed strongman against student dissent. The US also saw internal friction: a bipartisan briefing showed Russia targeting Democrats with misinformation, and top Trump advisers donated fees for work on behalf of a pro-Russian government after he floated firing them.

Putin also floated a proposal for a three-way summit with Trump and Xi in China to discuss the Ukraine deal, a move that would exclude Zelensky from the table. Trump said he was open to the idea and would focus on nuclear issues. This added a layer of great-power diplomacy to the already complex negotiations.
measurement.expected:
In the coming week, October 24 through 31, I expect the following:

Peace talks preparation and positioning: Almost certain. The Abu Dhabi trilateral meeting is set for early November, so the next week will be dominated by preparation, shuttle diplomacy, and public positioning by all three sides. Expect Witkoff or another US official to travel again, Zelensky to hold press conferences outlining Ukraine's demands, and the Kremlin to issue statements about what 'security for Russia, Ukraine and Europe' means in practice. There will be leaks and reporting on the agenda, likely including territorial questions, security guarantees, and the status of occupied territories. The Oleshky ceasefire will be a test case: if evacuation goes smoothly, it builds momentum; if it stalls, it becomes a flashpoint.

Continued military strikes: Almost certain. Despite the diplomatic track, both sides have shown no sign of reducing intensity. Russia will likely continue strikes on Ukrainian energy and digital infrastructure, especially ahead of winter. Ukraine will keep launching long-range drones at Russian refineries, airports, and data centers. The jet-powered drone base Russia built in six weeks suggests a new wave of attacks is coming. I expect at least one major strike on Kyiv or another large city, and one significant Ukrainian drone operation inside Russia. Casualties will be reported on both sides.

Diesel deal logistics and political fallout: Probable. The first tanker is already at sea, so next week will bring arrival at a US port, inspection, and the political reaction. Congressional hearings or statements about the legality and fairness of the waiver are likely. Oil markets will react to the actual delivery. The Novatek-funded US LNG project and the 25-billion-dollar gas venture controversy will generate more headlines as US executives and investors sort out their positions. Expect at least one more Republican or Democratic senator to publicly attack the deal.

Oleshky ceasefire implementation: Probable. The evacuation of civilians from the occupied town will be the practical test. I expect logistical hiccups, at least one incident (a stray shell, a disputed checkpoint), and competing narratives from Moscow and Kyiv about who is doing what. Melania Trump will likely be visible in the story, either through a statement or a photo op. The ceasefire is limited to one city, so I do not expect it to expand without a clear trigger.

Espionage and intelligence incidents: Possible. The pattern of arrests in Germany, Austria, and the detention of a Japanese journalist suggests a broader campaign. I would not be surprised to see one more arrest or diplomatic expulsion in a European capital. The Russian satellite's close approach to a US radar satellite may generate a formal diplomatic protest or a classified briefing to Congress. Poland's threat to fine social media firms may move from rhetoric to a specific regulatory action.

Putin-Trump-Xi summit: Possible discussion, unlikely to be scheduled. Putin has floated the idea, Trump has expressed openness, but the logistics of bringing three leaders together in China in less than a month are tight. I expect more statements and speculation than a confirmed date. If it is confirmed, it would be a major story. If it is not, the trilateral Abu Dhabi talks remain the main venue. I would not bet on the summit being finalized next week.

Economic indicators: Probable. The central bank's decision to hold rates at 14 percent and raise its inflation forecast will be digested by markets. The 60 percent jump in the tax-calculation oil price will affect the budget. I expect more reporting on how the war is straining Rosneft and other state enterprises. The halt at a major Baltic port will affect shipping schedules and insurance rates.

US domestic politics: Probable. The Republican backlash over the sanctions waiver and the Russia policy will intensify as midterm or primary positioning begins. The bipartisan briefing on Russian misinformation targeting Democrats will generate at least one more hearing or report. The 'Putin whisperers' narrative in the FT will fuel internal GOP debates.

Less likely surprises: A sudden Russian offer to expand the ceasefire beyond Oleshky (possible but would require a trigger); a second major prisoner exchange (possible if momentum builds); a Russian cyberattack on a US or European target that goes beyond Ukraine (possible, given the digital infrastructure focus); a formal EU response to the diesel deal, perhaps a trade or regulatory measure (possible but slow-moving); a Russian test of a new missile or drone system in the Black Sea or Baltic (possible as a signal before talks).

Things I would not bet on: A full ceasefire or a signed peace framework in the next seven days (the talks are not even scheduled until early November); a dramatic escalation such as a Russian strike on NATO territory or a Ukrainian strike deep into Russian industrial heartland that changes the war's character; a change in Russian leadership or a major Kremlin cabinet reshuffle; a Russian default or currency crisis triggered by the week's events; a confirmed Putin-Trump-Xi summit date with a specific location and agenda; a major Russian oil production cut or OPEC-style coordination that moves prices more than 5 percent in a single session.
emoji_reasons: The resumption of three-way peace talks, the Melania-brokered Oleshky ceasefire, the prisoner swap, and the Hubbard release all point to a genuine, if fragile, diplomatic thaw that defined the week.
Trump's sanctions waiver, the first Russian diesel tanker sailing for the US, the Novatek-funded US LNG venture, and the central bank's rate decision made energy and trade the central economic story.

Austria expelling four diplomats, a German spy arrest, a Japanese journalist detention, a Russian satellite stalking a US radar satellite, and Russia-linked hackers hitting Ukraine made espionage and intelligence the week's most persistent undercurrent.

delta.motion: Between the two photographs, the diplomatic track accelerated dramatically while the military track intensified in parallel, creating a week in which peace talks and cluster warheads on Kyiv arrived within hours of each other. The sanctions waiver and diesel deal, which in the first photograph was a political shock still being digested by Congress and European capitals, moved into operational reality in the second: the first tanker of Russian diesel physically sailed for the United States on October 23, Novatek's hidden funding of a US LNG project came to light, and senior executives quit a 25-billion-dollar gas venture over claims of secret Russian control. The story shifted from 'will this deal survive the political fight' to 'here is the tanker, here is the money, here are the people leaving.' The aerial tit-for-tat grew in scale and lethality. Where the first week saw a drone hit the Ryazan refinery and Russia strike steel plants across nine regions, the second week brought Ukraine launching over a thousand drones at Russia, setting multiple oil facilities ablaze and hitting the data center of Russia's largest bank, while Russia dropped cluster warheads on Kyiv and struck Moscow-area airports. The new Russian drone megabase, visible in satellite images in the first week, was confirmed as a build-out in the second, and North Korean workers were reported to be treated as slaves at a Russian drone factory, adding a labor and human-rights dimension that was absent before. The Black Sea and Baltic maritime thread, which in the first photograph was a cluster of incidents (Romania, Bulgaria, Poland reporting drone events near shipping), escalated into a concrete casualty event: Romania blamed Russia for a drone that sank a cargo ship, killing one person and leaving three missing. This is a step up from 'an incident near shipping lanes' to 'a ship actually sunk with bodies in the water.' The multilateral diplomatic venue shifted. The first photograph centered on the G20 in Bangkok as the expected stage for Russia's return to the table. The second photograph shows the G20 largely absent from the headlines; instead, the resumption of three-way talks in Abu Dhabi and Putin's floated proposal for a three-way summit with Trump and Xi in China took center stage. Russia's diplomacy moved from a multilateral, EU-adjacent context to a bilateral and trilateral great-power context that deliberately sidelines Zelensky. The espionage and information-war thread broadened geographically. The first week featured a Japanese journalist in the Far East and a Swedish man in a Russian jail. The second week added Austria expelling four Russian diplomats, a suspected spy arrested in Germany, a German man detained in Russia, a Russian military satellite making an unprecedented close approach to a US radar satellite, Poland threatening fines on social media firms, and Germany's military warning of a significant sabotage threat. The theater expanded from two small bilateral irritants to a Europe-wide and even orbital confrontation. On the economic and domestic front, the first photograph's items (Kamchatka earthquake, Novaya Gazeta investigation, A7 board appointment) largely faded from the headlines. In their place, the second photograph shows the central bank holding its rate at 14 percent while raising its inflation forecast, oil used for tax calculations jumping 60 percent above the budget level, Russia shipping the least oil in a month after a Baltic port halted operations, wheat exports being rerouted through a disputed region, Nestle removing Russian business from its accounts, and a temporary control of a metro unit being reported as a war-funding mechanism. The domestic story shifted from a one-off earthquake and a media investigation to a sustained macroeconomic and corporate picture. New themes appeared in the second photograph that had no counterpart in the first: the Oleshky one-city ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump, the release of 74-year-old American Stephen Hubbard after four years in a Russian jail, a 270-for-270 prisoner swap, Slovakia breaking with EU allies by restarting consultations with Russia, Hungary considering replacing Rosatom in a nuclear project, Finland seeking one million landmines, the EU unveiling a new Arctic strategy, Denmark ordering long-range missiles, and Human Rights Watch accusing Russia and its Mali allies of new atrocities. The Oleshky ceasefire and the Hubbard release, in particular, represent a human-scale de-escalation that was not present in the first week's narrative. Themes that shrank or vanished: the specific G20-in-Bangkok framing, the Kamchatka earthquake follow-up, the Novaya Gazeta editor questioning, and the particular US midterm bot-disinformation angle (which reappeared but in a broader bipartisan-briefing form). The overall motion is one of diplomacy accelerating into concrete meetings and gestures while the war simultaneously escalates in lethality and geographic spread, and the strategic competition widens from Ukraine's borders into the Arctic, orbit, and the Black Sea.
delta.wind: Theme by theme, the expectations were broadly correct in direction but underestimated both the speed of diplomatic progress and the severity of the military and maritime escalation. The sanctions and diesel deal aftermath was rated almost certain to remain the top diplomatic story, and it did, but in a more operational form than predicted: the first tanker sailed, Novatek's hidden funding was exposed, and executives quit a gas venture. The expectation mentioned congressional hearings and legal challenges, which continued, but the week's headline was the physical movement of the diesel and the corporate fallout, not the courtroom. The continued aerial tit-for-tat was rated almost certain, and it delivered: over a thousand Ukrainian drones, cluster warheads on Kyiv, data-center hits, and the drone megabase confirmed. This came true almost exactly as forecast, perhaps slightly more intensively than the 'at least one more major wave' language suggested. The Black Sea and Baltic maritime tension was rated probable for at least one more incident and possible for a more serious escalation. The reality was a cargo ship sunk in the Black Sea with one dead and three missing, blamed on Russia by Romania. This landed in the 'possible for a more serious escalation' bucket and arguably exceeded it, since a ship was actually lost with casualties rather than merely 'hit' or 'damaged.' The G20 and multilateral diplomacy was rated probable for at least one Russia-related headline and possible for a trilateral meeting. The trilateral meeting was indeed arranged (Abu Dhabi, early November), which was the 'possible' outcome, but it arrived faster and with more fanfare than the 'at least one headline' framing suggested. More notably, the G20 in Bangkok itself was not the headline; Putin's proposal for a three-way summit with Trump and Xi in China, which would exclude Zelensky, was a development not explicitly in the expectations. The espionage and information war was rated probable for at least one thread producing a new headline. It produced several, and they were broader in geographic scope (Austria, Germany, satellite in orbit, Poland's social media fines) than the Japan-Sweden-US-midterm framing of the first week. The nuclear and energy infrastructure theme was rated possible for a headline and unlikely for a breakthrough. It partially came true: Hungary considering replacing Rosatom is a new and significant development, but the specific Akkuyu start-up and Zaporizhzhia truce items that were named in the expectation did not dominate the second week's headlines. The domestic Russia items were rated possible for one or two international headlines. The central bank rate decision, the wheat export rerouting, and the Nestle and metro-unit stories filled that slot, but the Kamchatka earthquake and Novaya Gazeta items that were specifically named faded. On the 'less likely surprises' list, a one-city ceasefire (Oleshky) appeared, which is close to but not quite a full ceasefire. The 270-for-270 prisoner swap and the Hubbard release were not in any of the expectation categories and represent genuine additions. The North Korean workers at a Russian drone factory is another unlisted surprise. On the 'things I would not bet on' list, the expectations held well: no full ceasefire, no formal territorial concession, the Japanese journalist was not released, no major mobilization announcement, no confirmed nuclear test, no domestic political crisis making international headlines, and no second major earthquake. The main way the expectations were wrong was in underestimating the speed at which the diplomatic track would produce concrete, named meetings (Abu Dhabi, the St. Petersburg Witkoff-Putin meeting) and in underestimating the maritime escalation. The expectations also framed the week around the G20 as the diplomatic venue, when in fact the bilateral and trilateral US-Russia track, and Putin's proposed China summit, took over that role. The Oleshky ceasefire, the Hubbard release, and the prisoner swap were human-scale de-escalation gestures that the expectation did not anticipate, suggesting that the US-Russia bilateral channel is producing small, symbolic confidence-building steps that a multilateral framework would not. Finally, the expectation treated the espionage thread as a set of small bilateral irritants (Japan, Sweden) plus a US-midterm disinformation angle. The reality was a broader European and even orbital confrontation (Austria, Germany, satellite, Poland, Denmark), indicating that the hybrid-war dimension is widening faster than the week-one headlines suggested.
delta.driver: The force pushing Russia from the first photograph to the second is the collision between Trump's need to produce a visible peace credential before the US midterms and the war's own momentum, which refuses to pause for diplomacy. Trump's sanctions waiver and diesel deal were designed as an incentive for Putin to negotiate, and they worked in the sense that Putin agreed to resume three-way talks in Abu Dhabi and even floated a trilateral summit with Xi. But the same war that the deal was meant to slow down is accelerating: cluster warheads on Kyiv, a thousand drones, a cargo ship sunk in the Black Sea, and a drone megabase built in six weeks. Russia is simultaneously being handed economic relief (diesel flowing, oil tax calculations jumping 60 percent above budget, Novatek's LNG money) and being hit harder militarily (refineries ablaze, data centers struck, digital infrastructure targeted), which creates a paradox in which Moscow can accept the economic gift while still escalating on the ground, because the war is funding the war and the deal is not yet large enough to change the calculus on the front. The broader strategic competition is widening the theater: the Arctic strategy, the satellite close approach, the North Korean labor at the drone factory, the Mali atrocities, and the Europe-wide espionage wave (Austria, Germany, Poland, Denmark) all signal that Russia's rivalry with the West is no longer contained to Ukraine's borders but is spreading into orbit, the high north, and the domestic politics of every NATO member. The US-Russia bilateral channel, personified by Witkoff and Trump, is outpacing the multilateral channel (EU, G20), pulling Russia's diplomacy toward Washington and away from Europe, and producing small symbolic gestures (Oleshky, Hubbard, the prisoner swap) that a multilateral setting would not generate. The energy sector is the fulcrum of all of this: it is the prize of the deal, the target of the war, the source of the inflation pressure on the Russian economy, and the reason the central bank is holding rates while raising forecasts. In short, the driver is a two-track dynamic in which US-Russia bilateral diplomacy and the Ukraine war are accelerating in the same direction rather than in opposite ones, and the energy sector is the hinge on which both tracks turn.

Extending each theme along its motion: The diplomatic track has been accelerating for two consecutive weeks. Correcting for the wind: My last expectations were broadly correct in direction but I underestimated the speed of diplomatic progress, the severity of military and maritime escalation, and the breadth of the espionage thread. I was too conservative on the 'less likely surprises' list — the Oleshky ceasefire, the Hubbard release, and the prisoner swap all appeared and were not in any of my categories. The 'things I would not bet on' list held well. The key calibration lesson is that the US-Russia bilateral channel is producing more and faster than the multilateral framework, and that small human-scale de-escalation gestures are a recurring pattern I should expect again. I also need to weight the maritime escalation more heavily, since the motion went from 'incidents near shipping' to 'a ship sunk with bodies in the water' in one week.

What I would not bet on: a full ceasefire, a formal territorial concession, a major mobilization announcement, a confirmed nuclear test, a domestic political crisis making international headlines, the diesel tanker physically arriving (that is mid-November), a major natural disaster, or Russia formally changing its membership in a major international organization. These were all on the 'would not bet on' list last round and none materialized, and the motion does not suggest a sudden shift in any of them this week.

crystal.tldr: Next week will be dominated by the preparation for the Abu Dhabi three-way talks, with positioning statements from Moscow, Kyiv, and Washington, and the first concrete details of the agenda. The war will continue at high intensity with at least one more major wave of mutual strikes and a likely Black Sea incident. crystal.eli5:
Russia is in a weird and intense week. On one hand, the big leaders are trying to make peace: President Putin agreed to sit down with Ukraine and the United States in a city in the Middle East called Abu Dhabi, and that meeting is happening in a few days. So this week, all three countries are busy getting ready — figuring out what to talk about, who to send, and how to make it look like a win on TV. President Putin also suggested a meeting with the US and China leaders, which would be a big deal because it would mean three powerful countries talking about the war without Ukraine being at the table.

On the other hand, the war is not stopping. Russia and Ukraine are still hitting each other with drones and missiles. This week, Ukraine sent over a thousand drones at Russian oil plants and computer centers, and Russia dropped special bombs that scatter small pieces over a city. A boat got hit in the sea near Romania and one person died. So even though the leaders are talking about peace, the soldiers and drones are still doing their job.

There is also a big deal about oil and gas. The US agreed to buy Russian diesel fuel and let some Russian companies keep doing business in America. This made some US politicians angry, and some companies that were working with Russia are now having internal fights. Meanwhile, in Europe, countries are finding Russian spies or suspecting Russian hackers, and one Russian satellite got really close to a US satellite in space, which is unusual and a little scary. So the whole situation is: talking about peace, fighting hard, and dealing with money and spies all at the same time.
